strengths: This study enlightens the use of the MLE under correctly specified models.
The reported results are practically important because we can avoid using advanced methods for addressing the covariate shift problem.
The main strength of this study lies in the finite-sample minimax optimality of MLE under a covariate shift.
This paper tackles a well-motivated problem which has not been studied in prior work.
I believe it is a nice step towards understanding the sample complexity of learning parametric models under covariate shift.
It offers a comprehensive set of results, first tackling the well-specified case and then the mis-specified one, thus providing a clear picture of the state of the art in that area.

A nice feature of the result in the well-specified case is that it gives a tight answer about the sample complexity, identifying exactly how the mismatch in training and test distribution will impact the performance.
The paper is also written clearly, with claims that are explained adequately and there is a nice discussion about prior work.

The presentation of the covariate shift setting and the author's result is very clean and well-written, which is also reflected in the authors' choice of using linear, logistic models to illustrate their main result.
The upper and lower matching bounds on the MLE estimator is nicely presented with necessary conditions along with the MWLE estimator under the misspecified model, which imposes stronger conditions.
This is a technically solid paper, which demonstrates, for certain natural models, that the MLE achieves the minimax optimal sample complexity for covariate shift in the well-specified case.
The authors also apply their findings to several (generalized) linear models, which may have potential real-world applications.
The examples distinguishing between the well-specified and misspecified cases are also intriguing.
weaknesses: Although the points raised by the authors are practically important, I cannot find novel findings.

The covariate shift problem is not serious when models are correctly specified, and the idea that 'MLE is all we need' is already known to researchers, making the contribution on OOD under correctly specified models lacking novelty.
The claimed contribution of finite-sample minimax optimality of MLE under correctly specified parametric models appears to be already shown by existing studies with more general forms or is trivial.

Existing studies discuss the uniform or point-wise minimax optimality of estimation of f_\theta(x), which directly implies the minimax optimality under a covariate shift, suggesting the authors' results could be strengthened.

Some of the main results do not involve significant novelty on a technical level; for example, the proof of the upper bound follows using standard arguments in parametric estimation, similar to standard consistency arguments in parametric statistics.
The authors should provide more intuition on why simple MLE works so well in the well-specified model using purely source data.

The paper should cite and compare with relevant nonparametric covariate shift literature (e.g., conformal prediction papers) and discuss comparisons between prediction and estimation problems under covariate shift.

The paper might overly exaggerate its contributions; Theorem 3.1 is essentially a direct corollary of the introduced assumptions, which already state that the MLE converges to the optimal parameter—the very result the theorem claims to prove.
The paper limits its focus to only (generalized) linear models, a narrow scope that does not convincingly demonstrate that MLE is indeed "All You Need" for covariate shift.
The title exaggerates the claims; the authors should represent their results more accurately, possibly changing the title to reflect the actual contribution.
Assumption A and C apply to both the model class and the source and target distributions, not only to the model class as claimed by the authors.
In Section 4, it would be beneficial to also mention the lower bounds for each example.
The current length of the paper (50 pages) is excessive; providing an outline of the primary proof techniques would help readers distinguish essential steps from routine procedures.
